description: We are a team participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, interested in exploring innovative solutions through technology, creativity, and collaboration. We are particularly interested in Earth science, web development, data visualization, and audio technology. We welcome passionate members with skills in programming, UI/UX design, data analysis, sound design, and creative problem-solving who are eager to learn, collaborate, and build something meaningful together.
summary: Earth Sound Explorer is a prototype web app that turns Earth data into live sound, so people can hear how our planet is changing instead of only seeing it. Many Earth visualizations depend on sight, which leaves out people with visual impairments. In our app, temperature controls pitch, rainfall controls rhythm and wildfire activity controls loudness, and users can move through the years 2010-2025 or compare 2010 with 2025. The page explains which value drives each sound. This prototype uses illustrative sample values; the design is built to take real NASA Earth data as the next step. See the Earth. Hear the Earth. Understand the Changes.
details: What it does: Earth Sound Explorer is a prototype web app that turns Earth data into sound so that Earth science can be experienced by hearing as well as sight. It shows an Earth graphic that changes with the data, and plays live sound generated from it. How it works: - Data-to-sound mapping: temperature controls pitch, rainfall controls rhythm, and wildfire activity controls loudness. - Time travel through sound: users move a year slider (2010-2025) or press "Compare 2010 vs 2025" to hear how conditions change. - Understand what you hear: the page shows the data values and explains which value drives each sound. - Controls: play, pause, volume, and a live waveform. Data note: this prototype uses illustrative sample values that follow the general trends of NASA Earth observation records (temperature, precipitation, active fires). The mapping is built so real NASA datasets can be plugged in as the next step. Benefits: it makes Earth science more accessible to people with visual impairments, students and the general public. Tools: HTML, CSS, JavaScript and the Web Audio API. Sound is generated in the browser by code, not by AI audio tools. SI use: the AI assistant Claude was used for brainstorming the concept, writing and debugging the code, and drafting this text. The team reviewed and tested the result. Future work: use real NASA datasets, add a 3D globe, an "Earth Orchestra" layering more phenomena, and pair the sound with NASA Earth Information Center visualizations.
